lesson.section: 36. Lower Limb Arteries, Nerves, and Lymphatics

steps.title: Lower Limb Arteries, Nerves, and Lymphatics
steps.body: Lower limb arteries run external iliac to femoral to popliteal to anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Superficial lymphatics follow the great and small saphenous veins; deep lymphatics follow deep vessels.

steps.title: Relationships and functional organization
steps.body: Femoral artery gives profunda femoris and descending genicular branches. Profunda femoris gives medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries and perforating arteries. Popliteal artery gives genicular branches and divides into anterior and posterior tibial arteries. Anterior tibial artery continues as dorsalis pedis. Posterior tibial artery gives fibular artery and medial/lateral plantar arteries. Medial superficial lymph follows great saphenous to superficial inguinal nodes. Lateral/posterior superficial lymph follows small saphenous to popliteal nodes.

steps.title: How do perforating veins connect superficial and deep venous systems?
steps.body: Perforators pass through deep fascia between superficial veins and deep veins accompanying arteries. Valves and the muscle pump normally favor organized return toward the heart, while calf contraction compresses deep channels. The great and small saphenous veins are superficial routes with characteristic junctions, not substitutes for the deep system. Vessel names describe location and continuity, while flow depends on pressure and valve function. A useful lower-limb venous diagram includes fascia and perforators as well as the two named superficial veins.

steps.title: Apply the anatomy and resolve a common confusion
steps.body: Femoral artery becomes popliteal after the adductor hiatus, then supplies tibial routes toward the foot. Branching patterns vary, including the length of the tibioperoneal trunk. Dorsalis pedis continues the anterior tibial route; posterior tibial branches feed plantar circulation. Great saphenous travels anterior to the medial malleolus and toward superficial inguinal drainage, while small saphenous passes posterior to the lateral malleolus toward the popliteal region. Superficial and deep routes communicate but are not identical.
